narrative:
The model predicted a 65% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year grades had the strongest influence. Placing in the bottom decile of your class (compared to an average of 6th decile among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.3, well below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failing the bar. Working full-time while in law school was the third factor; this actually nudged the prediction slightly toward passing, but not enough to offset the other two.

In short, the model saw your early academic performance and college grades as clear signals that you would struggle with the bar exam, and this outweighed the small positive effect of planning to study full-time.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record. Consider retaking challenging courses, enrolling in a post-baccalaureate program, or gaining structured test-prep experience to raise both your grades and your expected bar-exam readiness before reapplying.
